netinterest-stretch: Something odd is happening: stocks keep climbing while bitcoin is down 30% this year and roughly half off its peak. More interesting is the explanation from Michael Saylor, the man who bet his entire company on bitcoin. His culprit: AI. Mega-deals like Google's and SpaceX's have vacuumed up hundreds of billions of dollars, money that would once have flowed into crypto. Crypto didn't cool off; something hotter showed up. Rubinstein then goes a level deeper. Saylor's company, Strategy, buys bitcoin with borrowed money and specially designed securities, the flagship being Stretch: a security whose dividend is continuously adjusted to keep its price pinned at $100. It has raised $10.5B this way. With bitcoin still sliding, the question of this piece is whether that elaborate funding tower can stay standing.
testa-nikkei: Testa is the closest thing Japan has to a retail trading legend: he started with day trading, compounded his way past 10 billion yen, and a million people follow his X account. So with the Nikkei crossing 70,000, Toyo Keizai asked him the question on everyone's mind: how far can this go? His answer, consistent with what he has said for years: forecasting the overall market is meaningless, and he has never made money by calling the index. What an individual investor can actually control, in his telling, is the choice of individual stocks and how much risk they carry, not where the Nikkei lands. The interview also covers how he reads the AI-semiconductor boom that is driving this market and how he thinks about the new NISA generation entering at all-time highs. The full text sits behind Toyo Keizai's paywall; the free portion gives you his framing.
emin-korea: Emin Yurumazu is one of the most-followed market voices in Japan: Turkish-born, ex-Nomura, and the commentator Japanese retail investors quote most on global macro. His thesis here is uncomfortable for Koreans and directly relevant to everyone in the AI trade: if the AI bubble bursts, the epicenter may not be the Nasdaq but Seoul. His reasoning runs on concentration. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix alone account for roughly half of the Korean index, meaning the entire market is effectively a leveraged bet on memory chips. On top of that sit sixteen leveraged ETFs tied to those same names, and margin debt at record highs. Then his favorite tell, the shoeshine-boy signal: when everyone from taxi drivers on down is talking about semiconductor stocks, the marginal buyer is already in. His warning is that the most concentrated market cracks first and hardest, and a Korean unwind wouldn't stay Korean: Japan and Taiwan, wired into the same supply chain and the same trade, would catch it next. The full piece is on his paid note (about 980 yen a month).
marks-privatecredit:
Howard Marks has weighed in on the first big wobble in private credit. His conclusion up front: this episode is sentiment and fund flows, not actual defaults. But he sees the shape of it matching the anatomy of a bubble he has written about for decades.
One thing to set straight first. The line "AI's first credit event" is a label the market and press attached, not Marks's own. He draws the opposite line, calling it flow and sentiment driven rather than credit deterioration.

## What is private credit, and why did it shake?
Private credit, or direct lending, is when funds lend straight to companies instead of banks or the bond market.
It is a lightly disclosed, hard-to-see market, and it has swelled from about 150 billion dollars two decades ago to roughly 2 trillion today.
Software loans loomed especially large inside it. By Marks's figures, software is 20 to 30 percent of direct lending, versus just 4 to 5 percent of high-yield bonds and 10 to 15 percent of syndicated loans.
The logic was that steady subscription revenue keeps these firms from failing. They were bought at around 20 times earnings, with heavy leverage layered on.

## Why would AI shake a loan?
Lay the bridge first. The premise of these loans was that a software company's position is hard to take away.
Then in November 2025 Anthropic shipped a powerful coding model, and by late January a wave of plug-ins followed, and the cost of writing code dropped. The moat that held the position started to give.
In early February 2026 investors all reached for the same question at once. Are these companies still safe?

## So did money actually get lost?
It did not. This is where the surface and the substance part ways.

But the share of loans trading cheap is rising, so the market is repricing fear ahead of any real default.@@Checked 2026-07-10 · PitchBook LCD (Morningstar LSTA Leveraged Loan Index)

What happened in February was a rush for the exits, not a default.
As redemption requests piled into semi-liquid funds, managers triggered the withdrawal limits built in, the redemption gates.
The gates worked as designed and headed off a fire sale. Apollo capped withdrawals at 5 percent after requests reached 11 percent.
A loop set in where blocking exits made people more nervous, but Marks reads this as a flow problem, not a solvency one.
He does add one caveat: it is worth asking whether the NAVs people exited at, the values the funds set themselves, were overstated.

## So what is Marks actually worried about?
His real warning sits elsewhere.

@@CMP@@The common reading|AI torched the software moats. Software debt is the next domino.|Marks's reading|The firms still pay their loans. This is sentiment, not defaults.

He points out that this stretch matches the anatomy of a bubble he has written about for decades.
Something new appears, it holds a grain of truth, early winners draw envy, possibility hardens into certainty, and low-standard latecomers push prices up.
The real problem is not one software loan. It is that the industry took in too much money and put it to work too fast, at standards that were too low. He points to the First Brands and Tricolor bankruptcies as the warning.
He closes with Buffett. What the wise man does in the beginning, the fool does in the end.
